pradeep|Chemistry|0|62|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Check each analogy; three hold and one does not.
**(a)** ✓ **true.** Internal energy depends on how much matter is present, so it is
**extensive**; pressure does not, so it is **intensive**. Halve the system and U halves while
P is unchanged.
**(b)** ✓ **true.** Heat and work separately depend on the **route** taken between two states,
so each is a **path function**. Their sum is ΔU, which depends only on the endpoints, so
q + w is a **state function** — this is the content of the first law.
**(c)** ✓ **true.** For an isolated system a positive ΔS means a spontaneous change, and
high temperature helps where ΔS is positive; a negative ΔS alone makes a process
non-spontaneous in an isolated system whatever the temperature.
**(d)** ✗ **false.** The claim is that S°(graphite) = 0 at 298 K. It is **not**. The third law
says the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero only at **0 K**; at 298 K graphite has
S° = **5·74 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**. The value quoted for CO₂, 213·6 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, is correct, which
makes the first half the error.
This is where entropy differs sharply from **enthalpy**. For enthalpy only *changes* can be
measured, so elements in their standard states are **assigned** ΔfH° = 0 by convention. For
entropy the third law supplies a genuine absolute zero point, so every substance — elements
included — has a definite positive S° at 298 K.
∴ analogy (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|6|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Melting at the melting point is a **reversible** change at constant temperature, so
**ΔS = q(rev) / T**
The options are quoted **per mole**, so the heat must be put on a molar basis too.
**Step 1 — heat absorbed per mole.** The figure given is for 1 g, and one mole of water is
18 g:
q = 335 J g⁻¹ × 18 g mol⁻¹ = **6030 J mol⁻¹**
**Step 2 — the temperature, in kelvin.** Melting occurs at 0 °C:
T = **273 K**
**Step 3 — divide.**
ΔS = 6030 / 273
= **22·1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹** ✓
The two steps that decide the answer are converting to a **molar** quantity — working with
335 J for one gram gives 335/273 = 1·2 J K⁻¹ **per gram**, which is option (a) wearing the
wrong unit — and remembering to divide by **T at all**, since quoting 335 itself is option (b).
The sign is positive, as it must be: a solid becoming a liquid gains disorder.
For comparison, the tabulated entropy of fusion of ice is **22·0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**, so the answer
matches the accepted value.
∴ 22·1 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

Note: the printed key gives (b), 335 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, which is simply the heat per gram with an
entropy unit attached. Dividing the molar heat by 273 K gives 22·1, so the key is wrong and
has been corrected to (c).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|7|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two conditions are imposed, and each kills one term of the first law.
**'Adiabatic'** means no heat crosses the boundary:
**q = 0**
**'Free expansion'** means the gas expands into a **vacuum**, so there is nothing pushing
back. The work is w = −P(ext) ΔV, and with P(ext) = 0,
**w = 0**
**Now apply the first law.**
ΔU = q + w = 0 + 0 = **0**
**And for an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature.** If ΔU = 0 then the temperature
cannot have changed:
**ΔT = 0**
So q = 0, ΔT = 0 and w = 0 ✓ — option (c).
This is the **Joule experiment**, and the result is at first surprising: the gas expands, yet
it neither cools nor does any work. The reason is that there are no intermolecular
attractions in an ideal gas, so spreading the molecules further apart costs no energy — and
with no opposing pressure, no work is extracted either.
A **real** gas behaves differently. Its molecules do attract one another, so free expansion
does cool it slightly — the Joule–Thomson effect, which is how gases are liquefied
industrially.
The distractors each keep one term alive: (a) has the temperature changing with no energy
flow, and (b) has heat crossing an adiabatic wall.
∴ q = 0, ΔT = 0, w = 0.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|8|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Compare the two paths on a pV diagram, remembering that **work is the area under the curve**
and that for compression the work is done **on** the gas, so w is **positive**.
**Irreversible compression.** The external pressure is raised **in one step** to the final
value and held there while the gas is squeezed from V(i) to V(f). The area under that
horizontal line is
w = −P(ext, final) × (V(f) − V(i))
Since P(ext) is at the **high** final pressure throughout, the area is **large**.
**Reversible compression.** The external pressure is kept only infinitesimally above the
gas pressure at every instant, so it starts low and rises gradually. The area under that
curve is **smaller**.
Therefore
**w(reversible) < w(irreversible)** ✓
The general principle: **reversible compression requires the minimum work**, and reversible
expansion delivers the maximum work. A reversible path is always the most economical,
because nothing is wasted on overcoming a pressure difference.
It is worth being careful with the sign convention, since it reverses the wording. In
magnitude, less work has to be spent compressing reversibly; with w positive for compression,
that is w(rev) < w(irrev), which is what option (b) says.
∴ w (reversible) < w (irreversible).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|20|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
For a mixture, the molar heat capacity is the **mole-weighted average** of the components'
values.
**Step 1 — Cv of each gas**, from the degrees of freedom:
**monatomic** (3 translational): Cv = (3/2)R = **3 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**
**diatomic** (3 translational + 2 rotational): Cv = (5/2)R = **5 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**
taking R ≈ 2 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
**Step 2 — weighted average.** With n₁ = n₂ = 1 mol,
Cv(mix) = (n₁Cv₁ + n₂Cv₂) / (n₁ + n₂)
= (1 × 3 + 1 × 5) / (1 + 1)
= 8 / 2
= **4 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓
The trap is option (c), 8 cal — that is the **total** heat capacity of the two moles together,
not the **molar** value the question asks for. Dividing by the total number of moles is the
step that distinguishes them.
A sanity check: the answer must lie **between** 3 and 5, since it is an average of the two,
and with equal amounts it must be exactly halfway. That alone rules out (b), (c) and (d).
The general formula is Cv(mix) = Σ nᵢCvᵢ / Σ nᵢ, and the same weighting applies to Cp.
∴ 4 cal.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|22|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Work out the molar heat capacity from the data, then match it to a type of gas.
**Step 1 — molar heat capacity.**
C = q / (n ΔT)
= 41·75 / (0·1 × 20)
= 41·75 / 2
= **20·875 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**
(A rise of 20 °C is a rise of 20 K, so no temperature conversion is needed for a difference.)
**Step 2 — compare with the theoretical values at constant volume.** With
R = 8·314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹:
**monatomic** Cv = (3/2)R = **12·47**
**diatomic** Cv = (5/2)R = **20·79** ✓ matches 20·875 almost exactly
**triatomic (linear)** Cv = (7/2)R ≈ 29·1
**polyatomic (non-linear)** Cv = 3R ≈ 24·9 or more
The measured 20·875 agrees with (5/2)R to within half a percent, so the gas is **diatomic** ✓
The reasoning behind the values is the **equipartition** of energy: each degree of freedom
contributes ½R. A monatomic gas has only 3 translational degrees of freedom, giving (3/2)R;
a diatomic molecule adds 2 rotational ones about the two axes perpendicular to the bond,
giving (5/2)R. (Vibration contributes only at high temperature.)
So the heat capacity is a direct probe of molecular shape, which is the point of the question.
∴ diatomic.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|23|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Step 1 — moles of argon.** Argon is **monatomic** with atomic mass 40, so
n = 40 / 40 = **1 mol**
**Step 2 — Cv for a monatomic gas.**
Cv = (3/2) R = (3/2) × 2 = **3 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹**
(The question supplies R = 2 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ precisely so this comes out whole.)
**Step 3 — temperature change.**
ΔT = 100 − 40 = **60 °C = 60 K**
**Step 4 — heat required at constant volume.**
q = n Cv ΔT
= 1 × 3 × 60
= **180 cal** ✓
Three things could go wrong and each has a distractor waiting. Using **Cp** instead of Cv —
Cp = (5/2)R = 5, giving 300 cal — would be the answer if the heating were at constant
pressure, but the question says constant **volume**, so no work is done and all the heat goes
into internal energy. Treating argon as diatomic gives Cv = 5 and again 300. And forgetting
to convert 40 g to **1 mole** inflates everything by a factor of 40, giving 7200.
Argon is a noble gas, hence monatomic — that is the fact the question expects you to supply.
∴ 180.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Take the three quantities in turn.
**q = 0** — 'adiabatically' means no heat crosses the boundary. ✓ in every option except (d).
**ΔU = nCv dT** — this holds for an ideal gas in **any** process, not just at constant volume.
The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so a change in temperature
always produces this change in U whatever the path. ✓
**W = nCv dT** — from the first law,
ΔU = q + W = 0 + W
so W = ΔU = **nCv dT** ✓
All three together give option **(a)**.
Now the others:
**(b)** sets W = 0, which would require constant volume — but the gas is **expanding**.
**(c)** sets ΔU = 0, which would require constant temperature; but an adiabatic expansion
**cools** the gas, because the work of expansion is paid for out of its internal energy.
That cooling is the whole character of an adiabatic expansion, and it is why compressed air
feels cold as it escapes, and why rising air cools and forms cloud.
Note the sign: for expansion dT is negative, so W is negative — work done **by** the gas, as
it should be.
∴ q = 0, W = nCv dT, ΔU = nCv dT.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|28|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two quantities are wanted and each has its own one-line formula.
**Step 1 — ΔU.** For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature:
ΔU = n Cv ΔT
= 5 × 28 × (200 − 100)
= 5 × 28 × 100
= 14 000 J
= **14 kJ** ✓
**Step 2 — Δ(pV).** For an ideal gas pV = nRT, so a change in pV is
Δ(pV) = n R ΔT
= 5 × 8·0 × 100
= 4000 J
= **4 kJ** ✓
So ΔU = 14 kJ and Δ(pV) = 4 kJ — option (b).
Neither formula needs the pressures or volumes themselves, only the **temperature change**,
which is why the question gives no pressure data at all. The word 'reversible' is likewise
not needed: both U and pV are **state functions**, so their changes depend only on the
initial and final states, not on the path taken. It is q and w that would require the path.
A useful by-product: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) = 14 + 4 = **18 kJ**, which also equals nCpΔT with
Cp = Cv + R = 36 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ ✓ — a good check that the two answers are mutually consistent.
∴ ΔU = 14 kJ, Δ(pV) = 4 kJ.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|29|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Start from the definition of enthalpy:
H = U + pV
So for any change,
ΔH = ΔU + Δ(pV) = ΔU + (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁)
That is the general statement. The question's version, **ΔH = ΔE + PΔV**, writes a **single**
P outside the bracket — which is only legitimate if the pressure is the **same** at the start
and the end, so that
p₂V₂ − p₁V₁ = P(V₂ − V₁) = PΔV
Therefore the condition is **constant pressure** ✓ — option (a).
Why the other options are wrong, and not merely incomplete:
**(b) constant temperature** is irrelevant; the pressure could still change and spoil the
factorisation.
**(c) constant temperature and pressure** and **(d) constant temperature, pressure and
composition** both include constant pressure, so the relation would hold — but they demand
**more** than is needed. The relation is valid at constant pressure alone, whatever happens
to the temperature or composition.
This is exactly why ΔH is the useful quantity for ordinary laboratory chemistry: reactions in
an open flask take place at the constant pressure of the atmosphere, so the heat measured is
ΔH directly. In a sealed bomb calorimeter, where the volume is fixed instead, the heat
measured is ΔU.
∴ constant pressure.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|30|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
A bomb calorimeter measures the heat released by watching the temperature of the surrounding
water rise.
**Step 1 — heat absorbed by the water.**
q = m × c × ΔT
= (18·94 kg = **18 940 g**) × 0·998 cal g⁻¹ deg⁻¹ × 0·632 deg
= 18 940 × 0·998 × 0·632
= **11 946 cal = 11·95 kcal**
That is the heat liberated by burning 1·89 g of benzoic acid.
**Step 2 — moles of benzoic acid.** C₆H₅COOH = C₇H₆O₂ has molar mass
(7 × 12) + (6 × 1) + (2 × 16) = **122 g mol⁻¹**
n = 1·89 / 122 = **0·01549 mol**
**Step 3 — heat of combustion per mole.**
= 11·95 / 0·01549
= **771·4 kcal mol⁻¹** ✓
The mass conversion is the step to watch: 18·94 **kg** is 18 940 g, and using 18·94 g would
make the answer a thousand times too small.
Benzoic acid is used because it is the **standard substance** for calibrating bomb
calorimeters — it is easy to obtain pure, stable in air, and burns completely, so its heat of
combustion is known very precisely.
∴ 771·4 kcal.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|35|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Step 1 — total moles of water gas.** At STP one mole occupies 22·4 L:
n(total) = 112 / 22·4 = **5 mol**
**Step 2 — split it.** The mixture is CO and H₂ in a **1 : 1 ratio by volume**, and for gases
volume ratio = mole ratio, so
n(CO) = **2·5 mol**,  n(H₂) = **2·5 mol**
**Step 3 — heat from each component.**
from CO: 2·5 × (−283) = **−707·5 kJ**
from H₂: 2·5 × (−241·8) = **−604·5 kJ**
**Step 4 — add.**
total = −707·5 − 604·5 = **−1312·0 kJ** ✓
The trap is treating 112 L as 5 moles of **each** gas rather than 5 moles in total; that
doubles everything and gives −2624 kJ. Option (d), −524·8, is what you get from 1 mole of
each instead of 2·5.
**Water gas** is made by blowing steam over red-hot coke, C + H₂O ⟶ CO + H₂, which produces
the two gases in exactly the 1 : 1 ratio the question specifies. It was once the standard
industrial fuel gas, and the calculation above — about 13·1 MJ per 112 L — is why.
∴ −1312·0 kJ.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|36|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two adjustments to the standard figure are needed: one for the **weak acid**, one for the
**dibasic base**.
**Step 1 — the standard value.** For a **strong** acid neutralised by a **strong** base the
enthalpy of neutralisation is a constant **−13·7 kcal mol⁻¹**, because the only reaction
actually occurring is
H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⟶ H₂O(l)
**Step 2 — correct for the weak acid.** Acetic acid is only partly ionised, so some of the
heat released must be **spent** dissociating it first. Its heat of dissociation is
+0·30 kcal mol⁻¹, so the net heat is smaller in magnitude:
ΔH = −13·7 + 0·30 = **−13·4 kcal** per mole of water formed
**Step 3 — correct for the dibasic base.** Ca(OH)₂ supplies **two** OH⁻ ions, so one mole of
it forms **two** moles of water:
ΔH = 2 × (−13·4) = **−26·8 kcal** ✓
Both corrections are needed, and each has its own distractor: stopping after step 2 gives
−13·4, option (a), and forgetting the dissociation but doubling gives −27·4, option (d).
The general rule: a weak acid or weak base always gives a **less exothermic** neutralisation
than −13·7 kcal mol⁻¹, by exactly its heat of dissociation.
∴ −26·8 kcal.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|38|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Count what bonds break and what bonds form **per monomer unit** as the chain grows.
n CH₂=CH₂ ⟶ –(CH₂–CH₂)ₙ–
**Bonds broken.** Each ethylene molecule gives up its **C=C** double bond:
n × 590 kJ
**Bonds formed.** In the polymer, 2n carbon atoms are joined in one long chain, which needs
**2n − 1 ≈ 2n** single C–C bonds:
2n × 331 kJ
**Net enthalpy change.**
ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed)
= 590n − 662n
= **−72n kJ**
So per mole of ethylene polymerised, **ΔH = −72 kJ mol⁻¹** ✓
The counting is the whole question. Each monomer contributes two carbons to the chain, so on
average **two** C–C bonds appear for every **one** C=C that disappears — one joining the two
carbons that were double-bonded, and one joining this unit to the next. Counting only one
C–C per monomer gives 590 − 331 = +259, which is option (a) and the commonest mistake.
The negative sign matters chemically: polymerisation is **exothermic**, which is why
industrial polythene reactors need careful cooling — a runaway polymerisation can be
explosive.
∴ −72 kJ mol⁻¹.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|39|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Work backwards from the muscular work required to the glucose that must supply it.
**Step 1 — work needed for five kilometres.**
150 kJ km⁻¹ × 5 km = **750 kJ**
**Step 2 — allow for the efficiency.** Only **30 %** of the energy released by the glucose is
available as muscular work, so the glucose must release more than 750 kJ:
energy required from glucose = 750 / 0·30 = **2500 kJ**
**Step 3 — moles of glucose.**
n = 2500 / 3000 = **0·833 mol**
**Step 4 — mass.** Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has molar mass
(6 × 12) + (12 × 1) + (6 × 16) = **180 g mol⁻¹**
mass = 0·833 × 180 = **150 g** ✓
The step that decides the answer is **dividing** by 0·30 rather than multiplying. Multiplying
gives 225 kJ, 0·075 mol and 13·5 g — far too little. The efficiency is a loss, so the fuel
consumed must be **larger** than the work done, and dividing is what makes it larger.
Option (e), 45 g, is the answer with no efficiency correction at all (750/3000 × 180), which
is the other natural slip.
A sense check: 150 g of glucose is about 2500 kJ, or 600 kilocalories — roughly what a brisk
five-kilometre walk really costs, so the figure is realistic.
∴ 150 g.
